q: Who is known as the "father of genetics"?
Gregor Johann Mendel is called the father of genetics for his pioneering hybridisation experiments on garden pea using statistical analysis.
Mendel conducted his hybridisation experiments on which plant?
Mendel chose the garden pea, Pisum sativum, because it was easy to cultivate and had several contrasting characters.
What did Mendel call the functional unit of inheritance that carries information to express a trait?
Mendel used the term "factor" for what we now call a gene, the functional unit of inheritance.
The genetic constitution of an organism is called its:
Genotype refers to the genetic makeup (e.g. TT, Tt, tt), whereas phenotype refers to the observable appearance.
The external, observable appearance of an organism (e.g. tall or dwarf) is called its:
Phenotype is the outward physical expression of a trait, such as tall or dwarf stem height in pea.
An organism with two identical alleles for a gene (e.g. TT or tt) is said to be:
Homozygous individuals carry two similar alleles of a gene, such as TT or tt.
An organism with two dissimilar alleles for a gene (e.g. Tt) is said to be:
Heterozygous individuals carry two dissimilar alleles for a gene, such as Tt.
For how many years did Mendel conduct his hybridisation experiments on garden pea?
Mendel's pea experiments spanned seven years, from 1856 to 1863.
In Mendel's pea experiments, which trait was dominant for pod colour?
For pod colour, green was dominant over yellow, as recorded in Mendel's seven contrasting character pairs.
The specific region on a chromosome where a gene resides is called its:
A locus (plural loci) is the specific location on a chromosome occupied by a gene or allele.
A cross between two homozygous individuals differing in a single character is called a:
A monohybrid cross involves parents differing in only one contrasting character, unlike a dihybrid cross which involves two.
A cross between an F1 individual and either of its parents is termed a:
A back cross is simply a cross between an F1 individual and one of its two parents, regardless of that parent's genotype.
A backcross between an F1/F2 hybrid of unknown genotype and its homozygous recessive parent is called a:
A test cross specifically uses a homozygous recessive parent to reveal whether the hybrid is homozygous or heterozygous dominant.
A backcross between an F1/F2 hybrid of unknown genotype and a homozygous dominant parent is called:
An out cross uses a homozygous dominant parent, unlike a test cross which uses a homozygous recessive parent.
For a dominant character to be completely expressed even in the presence of a recessive allele, the genotype must be:
A dominant allele expresses fully whether the genotype is heterozygous (Tt) or homozygous dominant (TT).
The removal of anthers from a flower before pollination, to prevent self-pollination, is called:
Emasculation is the removal of anthers from the female parent flower so that pollen from a chosen male parent can be applied instead.
Mendel's success is attributed in part to his novel use of which approach in the study of heredity?
Mendel was the first to apply statistical analysis and mathematical logic to biology, using a large sample size that gave his results credibility.
Mendel selected how many true-breeding lines, representing seven contrasting character pairs?
Mendel selected 14 true-breeding lines, which represented 7 pairs of contrasting characters.
In a monohybrid cross TT (tall) x tt (dwarf), the F1 generation is:
Crossing homozygous tall (TT) with homozygous dwarf (tt) gives an F1 that is entirely tall and heterozygous (Tt), since tall is dominant.
On selfing the F1 (Tt x Tt), the F2 phenotypic ratio for tall:dwarf is:
Selfing heterozygous F1 (Tt x Tt) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 3 tall : 1 dwarf, as the recessive dwarf trait reappears.
The F2 genotypic ratio in a monohybrid cross (TT:Tt:tt) is:
The F2 genotypic ratio from a Tt x Tt cross is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, even though the phenotypic ratio is 3:1.
Who devised the graphical grid method for predicting the genotypes of a cross?
The British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett devised the Punnett square, a grid method for calculating the probability of genotypes in a cross.
Mendel's Law of Dominance is based on which type of cross?
The Law of Dominance, along with the Law of Segregation, is based on Mendel's monohybrid cross experiments.
Which law states that the two alleles of a gene pair separate during gamete formation so that each gamete receives only one allele?
The Law of Segregation (Law of Purity of Gametes) states that the two alleles of a gene pair separate during gamete formation.
The Law of Segregation is also known as the:
The Law of Segregation is also called the Law of Purity of Gametes because each gamete carries only one, 'pure' allele of a gene pair.
In coat colour inheritance in guinea pigs, which allele is dominant?
In guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus), the black coat colour allele (B) is dominant over the white allele (b).
A homozygous parent (e.g. TT) produces gametes that are:
A homozygous parent like TT can only produce gametes carrying the T allele, since both its alleles are identical.
In guinea pigs, a cross between a homozygous black (BB) and a homozygous white (bb) guinea pig gives an F1 that is:
Since black (B) is dominant, BB x bb produces an F1 that is all black and heterozygous (Bb).
On selfing the F1 (Bb x Bb) guinea pigs, the F2 phenotypic ratio of black:white is:
Selfing heterozygous Bb guinea pigs gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 3 black : 1 white, the classic monohybrid ratio.
If a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is testcrossed with a homozygous recessive dwarf plant (tt), the expected phenotypic ratio of the progeny is:
A Tt x tt test cross produces gametes T and t from the heterozygote combining with t from the recessive parent, giving Tt (tall) and tt (dwarf) in equal 1:1 proportion.
A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is selfed and produces both tall and dwarf offspring. What can be concluded about the parent?
The appearance of dwarf offspring on selfing shows the parent carried a recessive allele, so it must have been heterozygous (Tt).
A dihybrid cross involves parents differing in how many pairs of contrasting characters?
A dihybrid cross is between two homozygous individuals differing in two pairs of contrasting characters, such as seed shape and seed colour.
In Mendel's dihybrid cross (RRYY x rryy), the F1 generation phenotype is:
Since Round and Yellow are both dominant, the F1 (RrYy) from RRYY x rryy shows the round, yellow phenotype.
The classic F2 phenotypic ratio obtained in a dihybrid cross is:
Selfing a dihybrid F1 (RrYy x RrYy) gives the characteristic F2 phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1.
In the dihybrid cross for seed shape and seed colour, which traits are dominant?
Round seed shape and yellow seed colour are the dominant traits over wrinkled and green respectively.
A heterozygous plant RrYy produces how many types of gametes?
A RrYy plant produces four types of gametes in equal proportion: RY, Ry, rY, and ry.
Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment is based on which type of cross?
Unlike the Laws of Dominance and Segregation, the Law of Independent Assortment is based on Mendel's dihybrid cross experiments.
Mendel published his findings in the proceedings of which society?
Mendel published his results in the 'Proceedings of the Natural History Society' of Brunn in 1865.
In the F2 of a dihybrid cross, the ratio of Round-Yellow : Round-Green : Wrinkled-Yellow : Wrinkled-Green is:
The dihybrid F2 phenotypic ratio is 9 Round-Yellow : 3 Round-Green : 3 Wrinkled-Yellow : 1 Wrinkled-Green.
The 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio arises from combining which two monohybrid ratios?
The 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio is the product of two independent monohybrid 3:1 ratios (3 Round:1 Wrinkled) x (3 Yellow:1 Green).
In the F2 of a dihybrid cross with 16 total combinations, how many individuals show entirely new (recombinant) combinations not seen in either parent?
Of the 16 F2 combinations, only RRYY (pure dominant) and rryy (pure recessive) match the parents; the remaining 14 are new recombinant combinations.
In the F2 generation of RrYy x RrYy, the genotype "RRYY" represents:
RRYY is homozygous dominant for both genes and matches the original pure dominant parent (RRYY).
In the F2 generation of RrYy x RrYy, the genotype "rryy" represents:
rryy is homozygous recessive for both genes, matching the original pure recessive parent (rryy).
The full F2 genotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross (RrYy x RrYy) is:
The complete dihybrid F2 genotypic ratio across all nine genotype classes is 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1.
Mendel published his work on pea plants in the year:
Mendel's classic paper on hybridisation in pea was published in 1865, though it went unrecognised until 1900.
A dihybrid test cross (RrYy x rryy) is expected to give a phenotypic ratio of:
A dihybrid test cross, crossing RrYy with the homozygous recessive rryy, gives a phenotypic ratio of 1:1:1:1 among the four phenotype classes.
How many distinct gamete combinations are possible in a Punnett square for a dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy?
Since each parent produces 4 gamete types, the Punnett square for RrYy x RrYy has 4 x 4 = 16 combinations.
In the dihybrid F2 generation, what fraction of the offspring is expected to be Round and Yellow in phenotype?
In the 9:3:3:1 ratio, the Round-Yellow phenotype makes up 9 out of 16 parts, i.e. 9/16 of the F2 offspring.
Incomplete dominance was discovered by which scientist, working on Mirabilis jalapa?
Carl Correns discovered incomplete dominance in 1903 while working on the four o'clock plant, Mirabilis jalapa.
In Mirabilis jalapa, a cross between red-flowered (RR) and white-flowered (rr) plants gives an F1 that is:
RR (red) x rr (white) gives an F1 that is entirely pink (Rr), an intermediate phenotype, illustrating incomplete dominance.
On selfing pink F1 Mirabilis plants, the F2 ratio of Red:Pink:White is:
Because dominance is incomplete, the F2 phenotypic ratio (1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White) equals the genotypic ratio (1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr).
In ABO blood group inheritance, how many alleles of gene "I" exist in the population?
The ABO blood group gene 'I' has three alleles: I-A, I-B, and i, making it a classic example of multiple allelism.
Who discovered the ABO blood group system?
Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood group system in 1901; its inheritance pattern was later worked out by Felix Bernstein in 1924.
Which relationship exists between the alleles I-A and I-B in the ABO blood group system?
I-A and I-B are co-dominant with each other; both are dominant over the allele i, which produces no sugar antigen.
Polygenic inheritance involves a trait controlled by:
Only genes on the X chromosome
Polygenic (multifactorial or quantitative) inheritance involves a trait controlled by three or more genes whose effects are additive.
Selfing the Blue F1 Andalusian fowl gives an F2 ratio of:
Since dominance is incomplete in Andalusian fowl, the F2 ratio is 1 Black : 2 Blue : 1 White, matching the underlying genotypic ratio.
Which ABO genotype corresponds to blood group "AB"?
The AB blood group arises from the genotype I-A I-B, in which both co-dominant alleles are expressed.
A person with genotype I-B i has which blood group phenotype?
Since I-B is dominant over i, the genotype I-B i produces the B blood group phenotype.
A person with blood group O must have the genotype:
Blood group O results only from the homozygous recessive genotype ii, since the i allele produces no sugar antigen.
Who worked out the precise inheritance pattern of the ABO blood group system?
Felix Bernstein worked out the inheritance pattern of the ABO blood group system in 1924, after Landsteiner's discovery of the system in 1901.
Selfing the Roan (RW) F1 cattle gives an F2 ratio of:
Since R and W are co-dominant, the F2 ratio matches the genotypic ratio: 1 Red (RR) : 2 Roan (RW) : 1 White (WW).
The sickle-cell haemoglobin allele Hb-S is best described, in relation to the normal allele Hb-A, as:
Hb-S is co-dominant with Hb-A; the heterozygote Hb-A Hb-S produces both types of haemoglobin, confirming co-dominance rather than dominance or blending.
PKU (phenylketonuria) results from a mutation affecting the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which normally converts:
Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; its absence in PKU causes phenylalanine to accumulate and convert instead to phenylpyruvic acid.
In an untreated PKU patient, the accumulation of phenylpyruvic acid in the brain primarily causes:
Phenylpyruvic acid accumulates in the brain of untreated PKU patients, leading to mental retardation, along with reduced pigmentation.
Which scientist obtained the first experimental proof of polygenic inheritance, using kernel colour in wheat?
Nilsson-Ehle provided the first experimental proof of polygenic inheritance by studying kernel colour in wheat.
Who is known as the "father of experimental genetics"?
Thomas Hunt Morgan, who worked extensively on Drosophila melanogaster, is called the father of experimental genetics and father of sex linkage.
Morgan's genetic experiments were primarily carried out on which organism?
Morgan used Drosophila melanogaster because it has a short life cycle, produces many progeny, and shows clear hereditary variations.
Which two scientists proposed that the behaviour of chromosomes parallels the behaviour of genes?
Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that chromosomes, like genes, occur in pairs and separate during gamete formation, forming the basis of the chromosomal theory.
Who used gene recombination frequency to map the relative positions of genes on a chromosome?
Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency as a measure of the physical distance between genes, creating the first genetic maps.
Chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes are called:
Autosomes are all chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes (allosomes), which are involved in sex determination.
During which phase of meiosis do homologous chromosome pairs separate randomly, forming the physical basis of independent assortment?
During Anaphase I of meiosis, homologous chromosome pairs aligned at the metaphase plate separate randomly, providing the physical basis for independent assortment.
In Morgan's Cross A (genes for body colour "y" and eye colour "w"), the recombination frequency observed was:
Morgan's Cross A between the yellow (y) and white (w) genes showed 98.7% parental type and only 1.3% recombinant type, indicating tight linkage.
In Morgan's Cross B (genes for eye colour "w" and wing size/miniature "m"), the recombination frequency observed was:
Morgan's Cross B between white (w) and miniature (m) genes showed 62.8% parental type and 37.2% recombinant type, indicating looser linkage.
Based on the recombination frequencies observed by Morgan, which pair of genes showed the tighter (stronger) linkage?
A lower recombination frequency indicates tighter linkage, so y and w (1.3% recombination) were more strongly linked than w and m (37.2% recombination).
What recombination frequency (in %) equals exactly 1 Morgan (M) of genetic map distance?
By definition, 100% crossing over between two linked genes corresponds to a genetic distance of 1 Morgan (M).
A recombination frequency of 10% between two linked genes corresponds to a genetic map distance of:
10% crossing over between two linked genes equals 1 deci Morgan (dM), while 1% equals 1 centiMorgan and 100% equals 1 Morgan.
Who discovered the genetic/chromosomal basis of sex determination while studying insects, observing structures he named "X bodies"?
Henking discovered the chromosomal basis of sex determination in insects, observing specific nuclear structures during spermatogenesis that he named X bodies.
The "X body" observed by Henking during spermatogenesis was later identified as:
The X body Henking observed was later shown to be a chromosome and was named the X chromosome.
Chromosomes directly involved in sex determination are collectively called:
Sex chromosomes, which are directly involved in sex determination, are collectively called allosomes.
In humans, the sex chromosome constitution of a female is:
Human females have the sex chromosome constitution XX, while males have XY.
In humans, the sex chromosome constitution of a male is:
Human males have the sex chromosome constitution XY, receiving an X from the mother and a Y from the father.
In the XO type of sex determination (e.g. grasshopper), the male has the constitution:
In the XO system, there is no Y chromosome; males have only one X chromosome (XO) while females are XX.
In the ZW type of sex determination, which sex is heterogametic?
In the ZW system, the female is heterogametic, having one Z and one W chromosome, while the male is homogametic (ZZ).
In honey bees, unfertilised eggs develop, via parthenogenesis, into:
In the haplodiploid system of honey bees, unfertilised eggs develop by parthenogenesis into haploid male drones.
In the XY type of sex determination in humans, all ova (egg cells) produced by the female carry:
Either X or Y in equal numbers
All ova produced by human females carry an X chromosome, since females are XX.
In human males, sperm cells produced are:
Human males are XY, so they produce two types of sperm in equal proportion: 50% carrying X and 50% carrying Y.
If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg in humans, the resulting zygote will develop into a:
Fertilisation by an X-bearing sperm produces an XX zygote, which develops into a female.
In the ZW system of sex determination, the male has the chromosome constitution:
In the ZW system, males are homogametic with a pair of Z chromosomes (ZZ), while females have one Z and one W.
Which group of organisms is an example of the ZW (female heterogametic) system?
Birds, along with some reptiles and fishes, show the ZW type of sex determination, where the female is the heterogametic sex.
"Male heterogamety" is best illustrated by which sex-determination systems?
Male heterogamety is seen in the XO and XY systems, where males produce two different types of gametes (with or without X, or with X or Y).
In honey bees, the number of chromosomes in a diploid female is stated to be:
Diploid honey bee females (queens and workers) have 32 chromosomes, twice the haploid number found in males.
In honey bees, the number of chromosomes in a haploid male (drone) is stated to be:
Haploid male drones in honey bees have 16 chromosomes, half the number found in diploid females.
In the haplodiploid system of honey bees, male drones produce sperm by:
Since drones are already haploid, they produce sperm by mitosis rather than meiosis.
Henking found that only what percentage of sperm obtained the "X body" structures after spermatogenesis?
Henking observed that only 50% of sperm produced after spermatogenesis contained the X body structures.
A mutation resulting from a change in a single base pair of DNA is called a:
A point mutation arises from a change in a single base pair of DNA, as seen in sickle-cell anaemia.
Sickle cell anaemia is an example of which type of mutation?
Sickle cell anaemia results from a point mutation, a single base-pair change in the beta globin gene.
In pedigree charts, a square symbol represents:
In standard pedigree notation, a square represents a male individual, while a circle represents a female.
In pedigree charts, a circle symbol represents:
A circle represents a female individual in standard pedigree chart notation.
In pedigree charts, a diamond symbol represents:
A diamond symbol is used in pedigree charts to represent an individual whose sex is not specified.
In pedigree charts, a completely filled (shaded) symbol represents:
A fully filled or shaded symbol in a pedigree chart indicates that the individual is affected by the trait being studied.
A double horizontal line joining a square and a circle in a pedigree indicates:
A double horizontal line connecting a square and a circle represents consanguineous mating, i.e. mating between relatives.
A diagonal line drawn through a pedigree symbol indicates that the individual is:
A diagonal line through a symbol in a pedigree chart indicates that the individual is deceased.
A small filled circle placed on a vertical line in a pedigree chart usually represents:
An abortion or stillbirth of unspecified sex
A small filled circle on a vertical line in a pedigree chart represents an abortion or stillbirth of unspecified sex.
A dot inside a circle or square, or a half-filled symbol, in a pedigree chart usually indicates:
A dot inside a symbol, or a half-filled shape, indicates that the individual is a carrier of the trait being studied.
Since the DNA helix runs continuously within a chromatid, an insertion or deletion mutation in the DNA sequence:
Has no effect on the chromosome
Affects the chromosome as a whole
Because the DNA double helix runs continuously in a chromatid, any insertion or deletion in the DNA sequence affects the chromosome as a whole.
Genetic disorders are broadly classified into:
Genetic disorders are broadly classified into Mendelian disorders, caused by mutation in a single gene, and Chromosomal disorders, caused by changes in chromosome…
Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder, caused by a defect in the gene for clotting Factor VIII.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited as a(n):
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked dominant disorder, in contrast to haemophilia and colour blindness which are X-linked recessive.
Hypertrichosis (hairs on the pinna of the ear) is an example of a:
Hypertrichosis is a Y-linked trait, so it is transmitted only from father to son and never appears in females.
Down's syndrome, first described by Langdon Down in 1866, is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, i.e. autosomal trisomy 21.
Klinefelter's syndrome is caused by which chromosomal constitution?
Klinefelter's syndrome results from an additional X chromosome, giving a chromosomal constitution of 47, XXY, an allosomal trisomy.
Turner's syndrome is caused by which chromosomal constitution?
Turner's syndrome results from the absence of one X chromosome, giving a chromosomal constitution of 45, XO, an allosomal monosomy.
Aneuploidy involving the loss of one chromosome from a homologous pair (2n-1) is called:
Monosomy (2n-1) is the loss of one chromosome from a homologous pair, while trisomy (2n+1) is the gain of an extra chromosome.
Sickle cell anaemia results from a base substitution on chromosome 11 that causes which amino acid change in the beta globin chain?
Valine replaced by Glutamic acid at position 6
Glutamic acid replaced by Valine at position 6
Glycine replaced by Alanine at position 6
Leucine replaced by Proline at position 6
In sickle cell anaemia, a GAG to GUG substitution causes Glutamic acid to be replaced by Valine at the sixth position of the beta globin chain.
The mutant sickle-cell haemoglobin polymerises and distorts the RBC into a sickle shape under conditions of:
Mutant sickle-cell haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen tension, causing the red blood cell to become sickle-shaped.
Alpha thalassemia is controlled by genes located on which chromosome, according to the source material?
Alpha thalassemia is caused by defects in two closely linked genes, HBA1 and HBA2, located on chromosome 16.
Beta thalassemia results from mutation in a single gene (HBB) located on which chromosome?
Beta thalassemia arises from mutation in the single HBB gene located on chromosome 11 of each parent.
Cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder, involves a defective gene located on:
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defective gene on chromosome 7.
The protein affected in Haemophilia A, essential for blood clotting, is:
Haemophilia A results from a defect in the gene encoding clotting Factor VIII, so even minor cuts can cause uncontrolled bleeding.
Colour blindness (red-green, Daltonism) occurs in approximately what percentage of human males, according to the source material?
Red-green colour blindness occurs in about 8% of males, compared to only about 0.4% of females, since females have two X chromosomes.
If a colour-blind (X-linked recessive) man and a carrier (heterozygous) woman have children, what is the expected proportion of colour-blind sons?
A carrier mother passes the recessive allele to half her sons on average, so 50% of sons are expected to be colour blind, regardless of the father's phenotype.
For an X-linked DOMINANT trait, if the father is affected, the expected outcome for his children is:
All daughters affected, but none of his sons
All sons affected, but none of his daughters
An affected father with an X-linked dominant trait passes his single mutant X to all his daughters (all affected) but passes his Y chromosome to his sons (none affected).
An F1 pea plant of unknown genotype is crossed back to its homozygous dominant (tall) parent. This type of cross is called:
A backcross between an F1/F2 hybrid and a homozygous dominant parent is specifically termed an out cross; a backcross with a homozygous recessive parent is a test cross.
In a pea plant, the specific region on a chromosome where the gene for seed shape resides is called its:
Locus is the specific region on a chromosome occupied by a gene; the alternate forms of that gene (round/wrinkled) are its alleles.
In the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy, how many of the 16 genotypic combinations are expected to be heterozygous at BOTH loci (RrYy)?
The F2 genotypic ratio is 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1; the doubly heterozygous class RrYy has a frequency of 4 out of 16, the largest single genotypic class.
The 9:3:3:1 dihybrid F2 ratio can be understood as arising from the combination of two independent monohybrid ratios. This is best represented as:
The 9:3:3:1 ratio is the product series of (3 Round : 1 Wrinkled) x (3 Yellow : 1 Green), reflecting the independent assortment of the two gene pairs.
If two genes on the same chromosome show 6% recombination frequency, the distance between them on the genetic map, as defined by Sturtevant, would be:
By definition, 1% recombination (crossing over) between two linked genes = 1 map unit = 1 Centi Morgan; therefore 6% recombination corresponds to 6 map units (6 cM).

In honey bees, a queen bee (diploid, 32 chromosomes) lays an unfertilised egg. What will this egg develop into, and by what process?
A diploid female worker, by fertilisation
A haploid male drone, by parthenogenesis
A diploid male drone, by fertilisation
In honey bees' haplodiploid system, unfertilised eggs develop into haploid males (drones, 16 chromosomes) via parthenogenesis, while fertilised eggs develop into…
In birds, which follow the ZW sex determination system, which sex is heterogametic (produces two types of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes)?
Neither sex, since birds lack sex chromosomes
In the ZW system, the female has one Z and one W chromosome (heterogametic, producing Z-bearing and W-bearing eggs), while the male has a pair of Z chromosomes…
Nitrous acid, a chemical mutagen, causes mutation primarily by acting as a deaminating agent that converts:
Nitrous acid is a deaminating agent that converts cytosine to uracil in DNA, altering the base-pairing and causing a point mutation.
A mutation arising from the deletion of a single base pair from a DNA sequence, shifting the reading frame of all subsequent codons, is called:
Frameshift mutations result from insertion or deletion of a base pair in the DNA sequence, which shifts the reading frame; a point mutation, by contrast, involves a…

A double horizontal line joining a square and a circle in a pedigree indicates consanguineous mating (mating between relatives), as opposed to a single horizontal…
